extracted.intended_audience: poets, students, and general readers interested in poetic form and free verse
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing or analysing free verse (vers libre) poems, focusing on rhythm, lineation, strophic organization, sound, diction, and the balance between freedom and formal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of prescribed meter or rhyme
rubrics_metrics.description: Free verse does not use a prescribed or regular meter or rhyme and is free 'when it is not primarily obtained by the metered line.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core characteristic: avoid imposing a predetermined metrical scheme or fixed rhyming pattern as the organizing principle. Note the caveat that free verse is 'not considered to be completely free'—lack of regular meter/rhyme is the defining difference from fixed forms, but absence alone does not guarantee quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the rhythm of natural or irregular speech (organic rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Free verse tends to follow the rhythm of natural or irregular speech; cadence is built upon 'organic rhythm' or the rhythm of the speaking voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose lines and cadences that reflect breathing and spoken phrasing rather than strict metrical feet. Prioritize phrasing that reads naturally aloud; consider breath units and conversational inflection to shape rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to formal elements (line, rhythm, strophes, cadences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although free verse lacks prescribed meter, it remains subject to elements of form: the poetic line, rhythm, strophes or strophic rhythms, stanzaic patterns, and rhythmic units or cadences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately use these formal elements to organize a poem — line breaks, stanza structure, recurring cadences — rather than assuming freedom means formlessness. Donald Hall: the form of free verse is as binding and as liberating as formal fixed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strophe and cadence as organizing units (vers libre practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: In vers libre the unit is the strophe (which may be the whole poem or only a part); vers libre is 'verse-formal based upon cadence' that allows lines to flow when read aloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize sections of the poem into strophes with their own internal cadence. Remy de Gourmont's advice: include, at regular intervals, a 'full and complete line' to reassure the ear and guide rhythm — use such anchors intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the ear: prioritize read-aloud effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Vers libre 'addresses the ear, not the eye.' Cadence should allow lines to 'flow as they will when read aloud by an intelligent reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test drafts by reading them aloud; focus on sound-driven shaping (pauses, cadences, breath). If a line or break jars when spoken, revise. The spoken/audible experience is a primary organizing criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal patterns of sound, diction, and association
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern and discipline are found in good free verse: the internal pattern of sounds, the choice of exact words, and the effect of associations give free verse its beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft phonetic patterns (alliteration, assonance, consonance), precise diction, and associative resonance across the poem to provide unity and musicality in lieu of regular meter. Avoid careless or generic phrasing that erodes internal cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of repetition and punctuation to create rhythm and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets (e.g., Walt Whitman) repeat phrases and use commas to create both a rhythm and structure in otherwise unmetered lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ rhetorical repetition, phrase refrains, and punctuation strategically to build musical patterns and structural markers. Overuse or mechanical repetition is an anti-pattern; these devices should serve rhetorical and rhythmic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-length variation should follow contours of thought and image
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of the line is long and short, oscillating with images used by the poet following the contours of his or her thoughts and is free rather than regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary line lengths intentionally to mirror cognitive or imagistic shifts; avoid random lineation. Use longer lines for expansive thought, shorter lines for emphasis or breath stops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an original, poem-specific metrical/formal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Vers libre practice is 'not the abandoning of pattern, but the creation of an original and complicated metrical form for each poem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a poem-specific system of recurring cadences, anchors, or patterns that provides internal coherence. Consistency of the chosen local system helps the poem feel disciplined rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline and musical structure — avoid formlessness
rubrics_metrics.description: Free verse has been described as requiring discipline; critics warn that it can be restrictive or, conversely, meaningless if undisciplined ('Writing free verse is like playing tennis with the net down').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain musical and structural intent—imagist and modernist practice shows free verse gains legitimacy through discipline. Anti-patterns include airy, insubstantial lines without internal pattern or musicality; aim for clarity of formal choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional use of traditional techniques for structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Although free verse requires no meter, rhyme, or other traditional techniques, a poet can still use them to create some sense of structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use meter, rhyme, stanza patterns, or caesura selectively as rhetorical or structural devices within a free-verse context. These tools may be deployed sparingly to produce emphasis or contrast, not to impose a fixed form unless deliberately chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-specific prosody considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Free verse and vers libre are not synonymous across languages: French tends to give equal weight to syllables, while English syllables vary in quantity according to stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt free-verse techniques to the prosodic norms of the language you write in: in English, attend to stress patterns; in syllable-weight languages, consider isosyllabism and different accenting. What 'reads' as natural cadence differs by language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory emphasis and synesthesia (vers libre tendencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vers libre is historically concerned with synesthesia — the harmony or equilibrium of sensation — and with sensory, imagistic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid sensory detail and cross-sensory associations to create moments of synesthetic resonance. Balance sensory richness with formal patterning so the poem remains cohesive rather than purely kaleidoscopic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain poetic distinction from prose while allowing proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Free verse may border on prose ('Free verse may be written as very beautiful prose; prose may be written as very beautiful free verse'), so the poet must sustain qualities that mark poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve lineation, cadence, compressed diction, and sonic shaping to distinguish a poem from prose even when sentences flow. Beware of turning the poem into unmodulated prose-paragraphs unless deliberately aiming for prose-poem effect.
